newsitem.title: USA: Research links breast cancer to DNA damage.
newsitem.headline: Research links breast cancer to DNA damage.

text.p: A team of researchers has discovered a strong link between damaged DNA and breast cancer, which they say could undermine prevailing theories about a breast cancer gene.
Unlike a gene or genes that would predispose a person to breast cancer, damaged DNA could potentially be prevented, or corrected in late stages before tumours appear, the researchers said.

"Much of the effort on breast cancer now is directed to looking for individual genes. What we're saying is this is probably an overemphasis," said lead researcher, Dr. Donald Malins, director of molecular epidemiology at the Pacific Northwest Research Foundation in Seattle.

"If you're told you have a cancer gene there is not much you can do about it. In the case of DNA damage, we believe there is promise one can roll back the damage before the cancer cells form," he said.
The findings are published in the Nov. 26 issue of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Malins said the research could help explain why 90 percent of breast cancer cases have not been linked to specific cancer genes.

The discovery two years ago of a gene that causes breast cancer stirred a flurry of excitement, but researchers have more recently been baffled by the large number of cancer cases they cannot link to a gene.

DNA becomes damaged, Malins said, by the action of so-called free radicals, or molecules that are highly reactive and often attack the body's genetic material. The body's production of free radicals is triggered both by natural substances such as oestrogen, as well as outside sources like pesticides.
"The evidence we have now indicates that the structural damage to DNA is pivotal in the transformation of normal breast tissue into cancerous tissue," said Dr. Malins.

With minimal DNA damage, he said a diet low in fat and high in anti-oxidant-rich fruits and vegetables may be sufficient to repair the damage. With more advanced damage, he said drugs could potentially be developed to deliver larger quantities of anti-oxidant molecules to the DNA.
